items.content:
RT @vxunderground: Have I seen AI generated malware? Yes.

Is it impressive? Ehhhh

Yeah, so basically it's an undeniable fact internet nerds are using AI for their goop. Malware developers who have historically been pretty good at malware development are suddenly churning out malware variations at lightning speed (or they're smoking methamphetamine).

Nooby poop goop developers are spreading malware which give the facade of sophistication, but it's not.

I can immediately tell when someone is using AI to make malware, who doesn't know what they're doing, because they'll do all sorts of goofy shit which any actually skilled malware developer would never do.

Examples:
- Leaving notes in stagers
- Leaving notes in encoded strings 
- Leaving notes in encrypted strings
- Stupid goop architectural decisions which make no sense and serve no purpose
- Attempts at obfuscation which ... aren't obfuscation at all
- Buggy code (uncharacteristically buggy, either they're brain dead or AI slop)
- Forgetting to insert C2s (literally seeing: "Insert_Weburl_Here")

I have yet to encounter some "god-tier" malware that leaves me shaking, screaming, crying, throwing up. The enhancements are just:
- More stagers
- Cross language interop (Lua to C++ to Python to C++, using several different languages to accomplish tasks)
- Faster code changes
- Dramatically improved phishing lures

In conclusion, it's making the smart goop guys faster, leaner, stinkier. It's making the noobs think they're smart, but they're being goofy

items.content:
nginx2root / CVE-2026-123007: our take after reading the Xint and Wiz writeups

Two teams independently built working unauthenticated RCE exploits against nginx. F5 confirms the bugs, and fixes are out (1.31.9 / 1.30.7). This is a serious one. Patch.

But the version number alone doesn't tell you whether a server is exposed.

The widely quoted "98.9% of nginx hosts are in the affected range" counts version strings. The two critical bugs (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633) sit in the HTTP/2 code. They can only be reached if HTTP/2 is enabled, and nginx doesn't enable it by default.

A server is exposed to them when all of this is true:
- nginx 1.9.5 to 1.31.8 (stable branch: up to 1.30.6), without a vendor backport
- HTTP/2 module compiled in (true for most distro packages)
- HTTP/2 enabled on a listener an attacker can reach

Check from outside:

curl -sI --http2 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' https://HOST/

"2" means HTTP/2 is on, "1.1" means it's off. Test the nginx itself, not a CDN in front of it.

Check on the server:

nginx -v
nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o with-http_v2_module
nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'listen.*http2|http2 +on'

No output from the last command means HTTP/2 is not enabled.

How common is HTTP/2 on nginx? We spot-checked a few hundred nginx HTTPS endpoints listed on Shodan: roughly two thirds negotiate it. So not 99%, but still millions of servers.

What to do:
- Update to 1.31.9 / 1.30.7 or your distro's fixed package. Distros backport, so check the advisory, not just nginx -v.
- Can't patch yet? Turn HTTP/2 off until you can.
- The same release fixes three more RCE bugs that need other features (resolver with a variable proxy_pass, HTTP/3, mail proxy). Patching covers those too.
